title: Design a distributed logging system
scopeHtml:
Scope: requirements, API, estimates, agents, Kafka buffer, indexing, storage tiers, query and tail, alerting.

Scope: requirements, API, estimates, agents, Kafka buffer, indexing, storage tiers, query and tail, alerting.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
A distributed logging system collects log lines from thousands of services and machines, stores them cheaply, and lets engineers search them in seconds during an incident. Think ELK/OpenSearch, Splunk, Datadog Logs, Grafana Loki, Google Cloud Logging. Logs are the last resort when metrics and traces do not explain a failure.

Functional requirements

  • Ingest logs from apps, containers, VMs, load balancers (text and structured JSON).
  • Search by time range, service, level and free text; filter and aggregate (count of ERROR per service).
  • Tail live logs ("follow") and create alerts on patterns.
  • Retention policies (hot 7 days, warm 30 days, cold 1 year), access control, redaction of secrets.

Non-functional requirements

  • Ingestion must be extremely available and never block the application (apps must not slow down because logging is slow).
  • Searchable within about 5 to 10 s of emission (near real time).
  • Write-heavy: reads are rare but urgent (during outages).
  • Cheap per GB: logs are huge, and most are never read.

Decision gravity. Decide first what is indexed (full-text on everything vs only labels) because index cost dominates the bill. Full-text indexing every line (Elasticsearch style) gives fast arbitrary search but costs 5 to 10x more storage and CPU than label-only indexing (Loki style). Changing later means re-ingesting data.

Everyday analogy. A giant filing system for every note every employee ever wrote; you rarely open it, but when the building is on fire you need one page quickly.

Common interview traps.

  • Not asking about volume, retention and query patterns first.
  • Letting logging block the request path.
  • Designing a database-per-service for logs.

notes.title: API
notes.html:
Ingest (agents):      POST /v1/logs/batch      (gzip, up to ~1 MB, or Kafka / OTLP directly)
Query (humans/tools): POST /v1/logs/search
Live tail:            GET  /v1/logs/tail (WebSocket / SSE)
Alerts:               POST /v1/alerts
POST /v1/logs/batch
Authorization: Bearer <ingest_token>
Content-Encoding: gzip
{ "source": { "service":"checkout", "host":"ip-10-1-4-7", "env":"prod", "region":"ap-south-1" },
  "entries": [
    { "ts": 1731150000123, "level":"ERROR", "msg":"payment failed", "traceId":"4bf92f35",
      "fields": { "orderId":"o_9001", "code":"CARD_DECLINED" } } ] }
202 Accepted { "accepted": 1, "batchId": "b_301" }
429 -> back off (Retry-After header)
POST /v1/logs/search
{ "query": "service:checkout AND level:ERROR AND \"payment failed\"",
  "from": "2026-11-09T10:00:00Z", "to": "2026-11-09T10:15:00Z",
  "limit": 100, "cursor": null, "orderBy": "ts desc" }
200 { "entries": [...], "next": "...", "scannedBytes": 3200000, "tookMs": 420 }

POST /v1/logs/aggregate
{ "query":"level:ERROR", "groupBy":["service"], "interval":"1m", "from":"...", "to":"..." }

Always require a time range in queries; an unbounded search is the fastest way to take down the cluster. Return scannedBytes so users see the cost.

Industry example. OpenTelemetry's OTLP is the open standard for shipping logs, metrics and traces; Loki accepts logs through a push API with labels; Elasticsearch's _bulk endpoint is the standard batched write.

Everyday analogy. Dropping a bundle of letters in a mailbox (batch ingest) and asking the archivist for "all letters from March mentioning refunds" (search).

Common interview traps.

  • Sending one HTTP request per log line.
  • Search APIs without time bounds or limits.
  • No back-pressure signal (429) for the agents.

notes.title: Estimates
notes.html:
Assume 10,000 hosts, 100 log lines/s each on average, 300 bytes per line.

Quantity Calculation Result
Ingest rate 10,000 x 100 1M lines/s
Bytes 1M x 300 B 300 MB/s, 26 TB/day raw
Compressed text compresses 5 to 10x ~3 to 5 TB/day
Peak 3x during incidents (error storms multiply logs) ~3M lines/s, 900 MB/s
Retention 7 days hot 26 TB x 7 / compression 2x (index overhead offsets) ~90 to 180 TB on SSD
Retention 1 year cold 4 TB x 365 ~1.5 PB object storage
Kafka buffer 900 MB/s peak, 24 h retention, compressed ~3x, RF 3 ~230 TB across the cluster
Queries maybe 5 per second, each scanning GBs CPU and IO bound, not QPS bound

What this tells you. It is a write-throughput and storage-cost problem. 1M lines/s needs a partitioned log (Kafka with 100+ partitions) and horizontally scaled indexers. Hot SSD for 7 days is expensive; everything older must go to object storage in a compressed, minimally indexed format.

Everyday analogy. A river of paper arrives every second; most is boxed and put in a warehouse, only the last week stays on your desk.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting incident-time bursts (error loops multiply log volume exactly when you need the system most).
  • Keeping all retention on SSD.
  • Ignoring replication overhead (3x).

notes.title: High-level design
notes.html:
Components

  • Agent on every host (Fluent Bit, Vector, Filebeat, OpenTelemetry Collector): tails files or container stdout, adds metadata (pod, namespace, host), batches, compresses, retries, spools to disk when the network is down.
  • Buffer: Kafka: decouples spikes from indexing; absorbs indexing outages; allows many consumers (indexer, archiver, alerting). Partition by service or hash of host to keep order per source.
  • Indexer workers: parse, enrich, redact, and write into the search store in bulk (5 to 10 MB batches).
  • Hot store: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, ClickHouse, or Loki chunks plus a small label index.
  • Cold store: Parquet or compressed chunks on S3, queried by Athena/Trino or the same query engine (scan on demand).
  • Alert engine: streaming rules (Flink or Kafka Streams) such as "more than 100 ERROR in 1 minute for checkout".

Decision gravity. Put Kafka between agents and indexers. Costs money and a bit of latency (about a second), but buys durability, replay (re-index after a mapping mistake) and protection of the search cluster from bursts. Alternative: agents write directly to the search store, simpler but one slow cluster drops logs. Reversible, but ripping the buffer out later is hard once the other consumers depend on it.

Industry examples. Netflix and Uber push logs through Kafka into Elasticsearch/ClickHouse pipelines (Uber moved its logging analytics from Elasticsearch to ClickHouse for cost and performance); Grafana Loki indexes only labels and stores compressed chunks in S3.

Everyday analogy. A loading dock with a big holding area (Kafka) between delivery trucks and the sorting machines.

Common interview traps.

  • Agents posting straight into the search cluster.
  • A single shared indexer pool where one noisy service starves the others.
  • No schema or required fields (timestamp, service, level).

notes.title: Deep dives
notes.html:
Collection agents and delivery guarantees

Agent tailing logic: remember the file offset (position DB), survive log rotation (inode tracking), read in batches. Delivery semantics: at-least-once by default. The agent commits its offset only after Kafka acknowledges, so crashes cause duplicates, not losses. Duplicates are handled by a unique ID per entry (hash of source, offset, timestamp) so the index can deduplicate or the user tolerates rare dupes.

# Fluent Bit sketch
[INPUT]   Name tail  Path /var/log/containers/*.log  Tag kube.*  DB /var/lib/flb/pos.db  Mem_Buf_Limit 50MB
[OUTPUT]  Name kafka Match kube.*  Brokers kafka-1:9092  Topics logs  rdkafka.compression.codec lz4
          rdkafka.queue.buffering.max.ms 200  Retry_Limit False

Do not block the app. The app writes to stdout or a local file (cheap). A slow pipeline then fills the agent's buffer, not the app's thread. If an in-process async appender is used (Log4j2 AsyncAppender, Logback AsyncAppender), configure a bounded queue with a drop-on-overflow policy so the app survives. Losing a debug log is cheaper than a stalled checkout.

Decision gravity. Choose "app never blocks, may drop under extreme pressure" and make drops visible via a counter metric. The alternative (never lose a line) risks outages from logging itself. Per-class policy: audit/security logs must not drop and should go on a separate, durable path.

Everyday analogy. Dropping a note in an outbox tray; the clerk collects it later, and the tray has a size limit.

Common interview traps.

  • Synchronous HTTP logging calls in the request thread.
  • Agent with unbounded memory buffer (OOM on the host).
  • Assuming exactly-once delivery.

Buffering with Kafka and partitioning

Topic logs (or one per environment/tier), 120 partitions, replication factor 3, retention 24 to 48 hours, LZ4 compression. Partition key: hash(service, host) so lines from one source stay ordered and load spreads. Hot services (a chatty one producing 40% of volume) can overwhelm a partition; add a random salt for those, or give them a dedicated topic.

Consumer scaling. Indexer instances in one consumer group, max parallelism equals partition count. A burst increases consumer lag; autoscale on lag (KEDA) and use that lag as the primary health metric ("logs are 40 s behind").

Production incident pattern. Symptom: engineers see no logs for 20 minutes during an outage. Metric: consumer lag climbing. Cause: an error storm made log volume 10x while the search cluster hit bulk-rejection (HTTP 429). Fix: Kafka absorbed it; scale indexers, sample or drop DEBUG, apply per-service rate limits, tail from Kafka directly for emergency viewing.

Decision gravity. Partition count is a one-way door in practice (increasing it breaks key ordering, decreasing is impossible), so overprovision modestly at creation.

Everyday analogy. Several checkout lanes: more lanes cope with a rush, but lane count is hard to change mid-day.

Common interview traps.

  • Few partitions capping parallelism.
  • Letting one noisy tenant take down everyone's logs (no quotas).
  • No lag alert on the logging pipeline itself.

Indexing and the hot store

For each entry: parse JSON, extract fields, redact secrets (card numbers, tokens, emails) with regexes in the indexer so the raw never lands in storage, then bulk-write.

Elasticsearch/OpenSearch approach

  • One index per day (or rollover at 50 GB per shard); shards sized 20 to 50 GB; 1 replica.
  • Index lifecycle (ILM): hot (SSD, writes) 1 to 2 days, warm (HDD, read-only, force-merged) up to 7 or 14 days, delete or snapshot to S3 after.
  • Mappings: ts date, service and level as keyword, msg as text, dynamic fields off or limited (mapping explosion of unique field names can crash the cluster; cap with index.mapping.total_fields.limit).
PUT _index_template/logs
{ "index_patterns":["logs-*"],
  "template":{ "settings":{"number_of_shards":24,"number_of_replicas":1,"refresh_interval":"5s"},
  "mappings":{"dynamic":false,"properties":{
     "ts":{"type":"date"},"service":{"type":"keyword"},"level":{"type":"keyword"},
     "msg":{"type":"text"},"traceId":{"type":"keyword"} } } } }

refresh_interval: 5s is the "near real time" knob; the default 1s creates tiny segments and costs write throughput.

Loki approach: index only labels (service, env, pod), store compressed log chunks, and grep the chunks at query time with parallel workers. 10x cheaper to store, slower for needle-in-haystack searches over wide ranges, so use labels to narrow first.

ClickHouse approach: columnar table ORDER BY (service, ts), partition by day, strong compression (10x+) and fast aggregations; text search through skip indexes (token bloom filter).

Decision gravity. The storage engine is a one-way door in cost terms. Full inverted index is flexible but expensive; labels-only is cheap but has weaker free-text search. Choose based on the query pattern: if 90% of queries are "service X in last 15 min plus a keyword", label-first is fine. Because Kafka keeps replayable logs, you can run two engines side by side during migration.

Everyday analogy. Either index every word of every page in a book (big index, fast lookup) or only label the chapters and skim inside the chapter.

Common interview traps.

  • Unbounded dynamic mappings (one new field name per request id).
  • Daily indices with 1 giant shard.
  • Claiming Elasticsearch is the only answer.

Storage tiers and retention

Tier   Age        Medium             Query speed   Relative cost
Hot    0-2 days   NVMe SSD           < 1 s         100%
Warm   2-14 days  HDD / cheap SSD    seconds       ~30%
Cold   14d-1y     S3 Parquet/chunks  10s of secs   ~3%
Frozen 1y+        Glacier            hours         ~1%

The archiver is a separate Kafka consumer writing batches of 128 MB files to S3 in a partitioned layout s3://logs/env=prod/service=checkout/dt=2026-11-09/hour=10/part-0001.parquet.zst. Time-partitioned paths let a cold query read only the relevant files. Compliance logs may need WORM (object lock).

Decision gravity. Retention is a business and legal decision (PCI, SOC2, GDPR "right to delete" conflicts with immutable archives). Keep PII out of logs by design; it is the only reliable fix. Retention lowered later saves money easily; raised later cannot recover deleted data (one-way in that direction).

Everyday analogy. Recent papers on the desk, older ones in the cabinet, ancient ones in the off-site warehouse.

Common interview traps.

  • Everything on SSD forever.
  • Many tiny S3 files (slow queries and request costs); batch to large files.
  • Storing PII in logs and then needing to delete it.

Query path and live tail

Query gateway: authenticates, enforces tenant isolation, requires a time range, rewrites to the hot store and/or cold store, applies a query budget (max scanned bytes, timeout 30 s, concurrency limits per user). Results stream back in pages.

Live tail: a separate consumer reads the Kafka topic filtered by the user's query and pushes matches over WebSocket; it never touches the index, so it is cheap and instant. Cap at a few hundred lines per second per tail.

Cost control: heavy queries run against the cold tier asynchronously ("your result will be ready in a minute") rather than on the hot cluster.

Decision gravity. Per-tenant query budgets are a policy (reversible) but they protect the shared cluster; without them one wide regex query can halt ingestion queries.

Everyday analogy. Search at a library: you must say which years you want, and the librarian refuses to carry out the whole archive.

Common interview traps.

  • Allowing leading-wildcard regex over a month of data.
  • Live tail implemented as repeated searches.
  • No tenant isolation (secrets in one team's logs visible to another).

Alerting and sampling

Stream the logs through Flink or Kafka Streams with windowed counts keyed by (service, pattern); fire when above a threshold; dedupe and route to PagerDuty/Slack. Prefer metrics for alerting (cheaper, more reliable) and use log-based alerts only for rare event types; convert hot log patterns to counters at the agent.

Sampling: keep 100% of WARN/ERROR, 10% of INFO, 1% of DEBUG, with trace-aware sampling so that if a request has an error, all its lines are kept (tail-based decision made at the collector). Always include traceId in each line so logs link to traces (OpenTelemetry).

Common interview traps.

  • Alerting from logs when a metric exists.
  • Random sampling that drops half of an erroring request's lines.

notes.title: What interviewers look for
notes.html:
• Pipeline thinking: agent, buffer, indexer, hot/cold store, query layer.
  • Numbers: 1M lines/s, TB/day, replication, retention costing.
  • Back-pressure and isolation: Kafka buffer, quotas, drops that never block apps.
  • Index trade-offs: full-text (Elasticsearch) vs label-only (Loki) vs columnar (ClickHouse), with cost reasoning.
  • Failure thinking: agent crash, network cut, indexer lag, 429s from the search cluster, error storm.
  • Seniors discuss PII redaction, multi-tenancy, query budgets, trace correlation, and moving to OpenTelemetry.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing technologies without costing them.
  • Forgetting security and retention.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Logging is a write-heavy, read-rarely, cost-dominated pipeline: agent, Kafka, indexer, hot store, cold store.
  • 10,000 hosts at 100 lines/s is 1M lines/s and 26 TB/day raw; tier storage to survive the bill.
  • Apps must never block on logging; agents spool, retry, and deliver at-least-once; use bounded queues and drops with visibility.
  • Kafka buys burst absorption and replay; scale indexers on consumer lag; isolate noisy tenants.
  • Pick the index strategy (inverted, label-only, columnar) from the query pattern; cap dynamic fields.
  • Enforce time-bounded queries and budgets; tail from Kafka; keep PII out of logs; alert from metrics where possible.

questions.subtopic: Why a buffer sits between agents and the search store
questions.promptHtml: In a logging pipeline, why put Kafka between the host agents and the indexers instead of letting agents write straight into Elasticsearch?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you think in terms of decoupling, burst absorption and failure isolation instead of drawing boxes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Logs are bursty and the search cluster is the slowest, most fragile part. Kafka is a durable, replayable buffer: it absorbs error storms, lets indexers be down or slow without losing lines, lets several consumers (indexer, archiver, alerting) read the same stream, and lets me replay after a mapping mistake. The cost is about a second of latency and a Kafka cluster to run.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without a buffer, one slow or rejecting search cluster (bulk 429s) pushes back to thousands of agents, which fill their memory and either drop logs or hurt hosts.

Direct:   Agent -> Search store        (store slow => agents drop or OOM)
Buffered: Agent -> Kafka -> Indexer -> Search store
                       \-> Archiver -> S3
                       \-> Alert engine

Kafka gives: durability (RF 3, 24 to 48 h retention), fan-out to many consumers, replay (re-index into a new mapping or a second engine), and lag as a single health metric ("logs are 40 s behind"). Indexers scale in a consumer group up to the partition count.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "for scalability" with no mechanism.
  • Forgetting the extra consumers (archiver, alerting) are half the reason.
  • Few partitions, which caps indexer parallelism.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does it cost? -> About 1 s extra latency, a cluster to run, and sizing: 900 MB/s peak x 24 h retention is hundreds of TB with RF 3.
  2. When would you skip Kafka? -> Small scale (a few hundred GB/day), where agents plus a managed ingest endpoint with its own queue is enough.
  3. Partition key? -> hash(service, host) for per-source ordering; salt or a dedicated topic for a chatty service.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "decouples and scales". Senior: names replay, multiple consumers, lag as the SLO metric, partition count as a near one-way door, and the tenant isolation (separate topics for noisy services).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that skipped the buffer lost an hour of logs during an outage because the search cluster rejected bulk writes exactly when error volume spiked.

questions.subtopic: Agent delivery guarantees without blocking the app
questions.promptHtml: What delivery guarantee does a log agent give, and how do you make sure logging never slows down the application that produces the logs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you separate "never block the request path" from "never lose a line", and know exactly-once is not on offer.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The app writes to stdout or a local file, which is cheap. The agent tails the file, remembers its offset, batches, and commits the offset only after Kafka acks, so a crash causes duplicates but not loss: at-least-once. Each entry gets a unique id so duplicates can be dropped at the index. If the pipeline is slow, the agent's bounded buffer fills, not the app's thread; in-process appenders use a bounded queue that drops on overflow, with a drop counter.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App -> file/stdout -> Agent (position DB, inode tracking) -> disk spool -> Kafka

The position DB survives restarts and log rotation (inode tracking). A disk spool covers network outages. Memory buffers are capped (Mem_Buf_Limit) so the agent cannot OOM the host. For an async appender (Log4j2/Logback AsyncAppender) choose a bounded queue with a discard policy: a lost DEBUG line costs less than a stalled checkout. Audit and security logs are different: they use a separate durable path that never drops.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Synchronous HTTP calls to the log service in the request thread.
  • Unbounded agent buffer.
  • Claiming exactly-once.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you dedupe? -> Id = hash(source, file offset, timestamp); index dedupes or users tolerate rare dupes.
  2. How do you know drops happen? -> A counter metric on queue overflow, alerted on.
  3. Which logs must never drop? -> Audit/security; send them on a separate durable, acked path and accept backpressure there.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use an async logger". Senior: offset commit ordering, disk spool, bounded queues with visible drops, and a per-class policy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A synchronous logging appender with a blocking queue froze a payment service for minutes when the log backend stalled.

questions.contextHtml: You are asked to size logging for a mid-size company: 2,000 hosts, average 60 lines/s each, 250 bytes per line. Incident mode multiplies volume by 4. Requirements: 7 days searchable on SSD, 1 year cold, Kafka buffer of 24 h at peak. Text compresses about 6x; index overhead roughly offsets compression for hot data; Kafka RF is 3.
questions.promptHtml: Give the ingest rate, daily volume, hot and cold storage and Kafka size, and say what you would cut first if the bill is too high.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Quotes "about a TB" with no arithmetic, forgets the 4x incident peak and Kafka replication, and puts a year on SSD.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do queries need full-text or mostly service plus time? (decides the engine). Is there a compliance retention? Are there audit logs that cannot be dropped?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I state assumptions and keep every number visible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cost is driven by (a) index overhead on hot, (b) retention on SSD, (c) debug volume.
  4. How I'd verify each: The math.
Rate     2,000 x 60 = 120k lines/s ; peak x4 = 480k lines/s
Bytes    120k x 250 B = 30 MB/s = ~2.6 TB/day raw ; peak 120 MB/s
Hot 7d   2.6 TB x 7 = 18 TB raw ; index offsets compression => ~18 to 36 TB SSD (+1 replica = up to ~70 TB)
Cold 1y  2.6 TB / 6 x 365 = ~160 TB object storage
Kafka    120 MB/s x 86,400 = ~10 TB/day raw; /3 compression, x RF 3 => ~10 TB
         (using peak 120 MB/s as sustained for 24 h is the conservative number)
  1. Root cause: n/a; the shape is write-throughput plus storage cost, queries are rare.
  2. Fix (what I'd cut first): Sample DEBUG/INFO (keep 100% WARN/ERROR), move warm data to HDD after 2 days, label-only index for noisy services, drop unused fields.
  3. Prevention: Per-team volume quotas and a cost dashboard in GB/day per service.
  4. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not shorten audit retention to save money (legal), and I would not skip the incident 4x factor.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Traffic doubles in a quarter? -> Hot SSD and Kafka double; scale indexers on lag, add partitions early (cheap before data exists).
  • Query rate? -> Maybe 5/s, but each scans GBs: CPU and IO bound, protect with budgets.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team sized for average load; the first major outage 5x'd log volume and the pipeline lagged 40 minutes during the incident, exactly when the logs were needed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no arithmetic or only average load.
  • Hire: correct rate, daily volume, tiering, Kafka with RF.
  • Strong hire: also peak factor, index overhead, cost cuts ranked, quotas.

questions.contextHtml: During a checkout outage engineers report no logs for the last 20 minutes. Dashboards show: Kafka cluster healthy, broker CPU 35%, topic logs consumer lag for group indexer at 480M messages and rising. Indexer logs show repeated bulk rejected: es_rejected_execution_exception (429). Search cluster write thread pool queue is full. Log volume is 10x normal because a retry loop is logging a stack trace per attempt. A teammate wants to restart Kafka.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do right now, and what is the root cause?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Restarts Kafka (the red herring), or adds indexers, which only increases 429s.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the lag across all partitions or a few (hot service)? Did mapping or shard count change recently? Is anything else writing to the cluster (reindex, heavy queries)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Give engineers visibility now: tail straight from Kafka with a filtered consumer for the affected service. Then reduce load: drop or sample DEBUG/INFO for the storming service, rate-limit that tenant.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 10x volume exceeds sustained bulk indexing throughput, (b) one noisy service dominating a few partitions, (c) merge or refresh pressure from 1 s refresh, (d) a heavy query competing. Kafka itself is healthy so it is not the cause.
  4. How I'd verify each: kafka-consumer-groups --describe for per-partition lag; GET _cat/thread_pool/write?v; per-service volume from agent metrics; check refresh_interval and bulk size.
  5. Root cause: An error storm overran the search cluster's write capacity; Kafka absorbed it (that is its job), but nothing shed load at the source.
  6. Fix: Short-term: sample/drop noisy lines, raise bulk size to 5 to 10 MB, refresh_interval 5s, add data nodes. Long-term: per-service quotas at the agent, separate topic and indexer group for high-volume tenants, autoscale indexers on lag only if the cluster has headroom.
  7. Prevention: Alert on pipeline lag in seconds (SLO: 30 s), 429 rate, per-service GB/s; load test at 5x.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not restart Kafka, nor scale indexers blindly (more writers into a saturated cluster). Dropping DEBUG is acceptable; dropping ERROR is not.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Lag will take hours to drain; what then? -> Prioritize: a fast-lane topic for ERROR and recent data, backfill old DEBUG later or skip it.
  • Retention is 24 h and lag is 20 h? -> Consumers lose data when offsets expire; extend retention temporarily or skip ahead.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A stack-trace-per-retry loop made one service 60% of all volume; quotas per service turned the next storm into one team's problem instead of everyone's.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts components, adds capacity blindly.
  • Hire: identifies 429s, sheds load, tails from Kafka.
  • Strong hire: quotas, lag SLO, topic isolation, retention vs lag risk.

questions.contextHtml: The interviewer says only: "Design logging for our company. We have a lot of microservices and engineers complain they cannot find anything." No numbers, no stack named.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Immediately draws ELK with Kafka, no questions, no numbers, no mention of cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Hosts/services and lines per second (sizes the pipeline). Typical query: "service X, last 15 min, keyword" or wide forensics over weeks (decides full-text vs label-only index). Retention and compliance (PCI, GDPR). Structured JSON today or free text? Who reads: on-call engineers, security, product analytics? Search freshness: 5 to 10 s enough?
  2. Immediate mitigation: "Cannot find anything" may be a missing-field problem (no service name, no traceId) rather than a tool problem; I'd first propose required fields: ts, service, level, traceId.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Pain is (a) inconsistent format, (b) slow or missing search, (c) retention too short, (d) logs split across tools.
  4. How I'd verify each: Sample five recent incidents and ask how the responder looked for logs.
  5. Root cause: Decided after the answers; I restate requirements: ingest never blocks apps, searchable in 10 s, cheap per GB.
  6. Fix: Propose the pipeline agent, Kafka, indexer, hot 7 d, cold 1 y with the numbers once given, and state the index choice as the main cost decision.
  7. Prevention: Logging standard and a lint for required fields.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not pick a vendor before numbers; I'd not index every field.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Assume 10,000 hosts, 100 lines/s." -> 1M lines/s, 26 TB/day raw; go to the estimates.
  • "Budget is tiny." -> Label-first index plus object storage.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A new log platform was built before anyone agreed on a service-name field; half of all searches still failed because the data lacked the dimension people filtered on.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: no questions.
  • Hire: asks scale, queries, retention.
  • Strong hire: ties each answer to a design decision and questions the root complaint.

questions.contextHtml:
The Elasticsearch cluster turns slow, master node GC is long, and indexers log Limit of total fields [1000] has been exceeded for some indices. A new service logs requests like this, and the template allows dynamic fields:

{ "ts":1731150000123, "service":"search-api", "level":"INFO", "msg":"query done",
  "fields": { "req_9f31a": 12, "req_77be2": 9, "tenant_41": "ok" } }
PUT _index_template/logs
{ "index_patterns":["logs-*"],
  "template":{ "mappings":{ "dynamic":true } } }

Cluster state is 900 MB. Daily indices have a single shard each.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix it without losing data?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Raises total_fields.limit to 100,000, which makes the cluster state bigger and the outage worse.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which service creates field names? Can we change it quickly? Do we need to search by those values?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route that service to a quarantine index or drop the fields object at the indexer; roll over the bad index.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Unique values used as field names (a mapping explosion), dynamic mapping on, single giant shard per day.
  4. How I'd verify each: GET logs-*/_mapping and count fields; GET _cluster/state size; _cat/shards sizes.
  5. Root cause: Every unique key adds a mapping entry kept in cluster state on all nodes, so memory, GC and master updates blow up.
  6. Fix: dynamic:false (or strict) and explicit properties; store key-value pairs as [{k,v}] or a flattened field; fix the service to log ids as values; shard to 20 to 50 GB per shard; keep the field cap as a guardrail.
  7. Prevention: Template reviewed in CI, a field-count alert, an indexer rule that drops fields not in the schema.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just raise the limit. dynamic:false means unmapped fields are stored but not searchable, which is the right default.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need to search those fields? -> Use flattened type or move the key into a value.
  • Reindex from where? -> Replay from Kafka retention or from S3 archive.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One feature flag library emitted a field per user id; the cluster fell over at 3 a.m. and fixing it was a one-line template change nobody had reviewed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raise the limit.
  • Hire: identifies field-name explosion, sets dynamic false.
  • Strong hire: flattened, CI guardrail, shard sizing, replay.

questions.contextHtml: Elasticsearch hot storage costs 70% of the observability bill: 90 TB hot SSD at 26 TB/day raw. Query analysis shows 92% of queries are "service + level + 15 min window + keyword"; 3% scan weeks. The team proposes moving to Loki-style label index with chunks in S3, or ClickHouse. Engineers use the tool during incidents and cannot lose it. Kafka retains 48 h.
questions.promptHtml: Choose a target and describe a safe migration. Is this reversible?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch over the weekend", or declares one engine objectively best.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the 3% wide queries tolerable at 10 to 60 s? Is free text search on arbitrary history a hard need? Team skills and ops capacity? Compliance needs on retained data?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is planned work. Quick win: reduce hot retention from 7 to 3 days and force_merge warm.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Label-first (Loki) fits the dominant query pattern and cuts storage roughly 10x; ClickHouse is better if aggregations and structured analytics matter; Elasticsearch stays if full-text is critical.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay a week of real queries against a pilot of each engine; compare p95 latency, scanned bytes and cost per GB.
  5. Root cause: n/a; cost model mismatch between index everything and the query pattern.
  6. Fix (plan): Add a second indexer consumer group on the same Kafka topic writing to the new engine (dual write via the stream, no app changes), backfill from S3 Parquet, compare results on sampled queries, move a team at a time behind the query gateway, keep ES for 2 weeks as fallback, then decommission.
  7. Prevention: Query gateway abstracts the engine; cost per GB dashboard.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The data plane is reversible because Kafka and S3 keep the raw logs; the real one-way door is human habit and dashboards built on query syntax. I would not do big-bang cutover.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Mid-migration both engines lag? -> Independent consumer groups; lag is per group.
  • Engineers miss regex search? -> Label narrow first; offer async cold queries.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration succeeded technically but stalled adoption because saved queries and alerts used the old query language; they built a translation layer first.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: big-bang or engine fandom.
  • Hire: parallel run from Kafka.
  • Strong hire: query-pattern evidence, cost numbers, query gateway, reversibility reasoning.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review. At 14:05 an engineer ran msg:*timeout* over 30 days. Search cluster CPU hit 100%, search thread pool queue depth 800, bulk indexing latency rose from 80 ms to 9 s, indexer consumer lag climbed to 12 minutes. The query returned after 9 minutes; the engineer retried twice. Another team's secrets appeared in the results because all teams share one index pattern.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: causes, fixes, and what to change in the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the engineer and adds "please don't run big queries".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are queries governed at all (time range required, limits)? Is tenant isolation enforced? Are queries and writes sharing nodes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cancel the task (_tasks API), then block leading wildcards; restore indexing priority.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: No query budget, shared nodes for search and ingest, no tenant filter in the gateway, no cold-tier route for wide scans.
  4. How I'd verify each: Slow log, task management API, gateway audit log showing user, query, scanned bytes.
  5. Root cause: A systems gap, not a person: the gateway allowed an unbounded expensive query on the same hardware that serves ingestion.
  6. Fix: Query gateway enforces mandatory time range, max time span, max scanned bytes, 30 s timeout, per-user concurrency; reject leading-wildcard regex; row-level tenant filter; wide queries run async on the cold tier (Athena/Trino); coordinating nodes separate from data nodes, or a dedicated search tier.
  7. Prevention: Alert on search queue depth, scannedBytes, lag; game-day with a heavy query.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Budgets annoy power users; reversible policy, provide an escape hatch via async jobs. I would not rely on documentation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The secrets exposure? -> Treat as a security incident: redact at the indexer, per-team indices or filtered aliases, rotate leaked secrets.
  • Users bypass gateway? -> Block direct cluster access at the network layer.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After adding budgets, p95 ingestion lag stayed flat even during an audit week where analysts ran hundreds of wide queries through the async lane.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blameful, no design change.
  • Hire: budgets and time range.
  • Strong hire: isolation, async cold lane, tenant security, detection and drills.
